cxagents.plain: A customer-service AI agent is a program built around a large language model (LLM) that talks to a company's customers in chat, email or on the phone. It answers questions from the company's help content and can take a small number of actions through tools, such as looking up an order or issuing a refund. When it cannot or should not help, it hands the conversation to a human agent. Containment means the conversation ended without a human; resolution means the customer's problem was actually solved. This topic applies what you learned in Tool use, Guardrails and Evals to the most common kind of deployment an FDE works on.
cxagents.analogy: Think of a new employee on the help desk with a thick binder of procedures, a few buttons on their screen and a supervisor down the hall. You teach them the binder, you decide which buttons they may press and how far, and you tell them exactly when to walk a customer over to the supervisor with a note so the customer never repeats the story.
cxagents.why: Customer service is one of the largest areas where companies deploy AI agents, and FDEs are hired to make those agents work on a specific company's policies, systems and customers. A home-goods retailer might ask for an agent that handles 'where is my order' and returns by next quarter. Getting it right means reading their standard operating procedures, wiring their order system safely, designing the handoff to their human team and proving quality before a single real customer sees it.

subtopics.title: Turning SOPs and policies into agent instructions
subtopics.body:
A standard operating procedure (SOP) is the document a support team already follows: how to verify a caller, what the returns window is, when to escalate. It is the best starting point for an agent because the business has already agreed on it. Your first job is to collect every SOP, macro (a saved reply template) and policy page for the use cases in scope, and to find the person who owns each one.

Read each rule and decide where it belongs. There are three homes. An instruction goes into the system prompt: tone, what topics to handle, what to explain before acting. A tool limit goes into code, because it must hold even if the model is tricked: the refund cap, the identity check, the return window. An escalation trigger says when to hand off: a legal threat, an injury, a customer asking for a person.

Write the prompt in plain numbered rules and cite the SOP version, so when the policy changes you know which lines to update. Keep scope narrow: an agent that does three things well beats one that does twenty badly. Rules the SOP does not cover are gaps; ask the owner instead of inventing policy.

Edge cases to look for: rules that conflict between two documents, unwritten habits ("we always refund shipping if the customer is upset"), and rules that depend on data the agent cannot see.
subtopics.example: Brindlecove Home, an online homeware shop, gives the FDE a 14-page returns SOP. The FDE finds 11 rules. Four become prompt instructions (explain the 30-day window before starting a return), four become tool checks (verified customer, window, order total, 150 auto-approve limit) and three become handoff triggers (damage, injury, asks for a person). Two rules conflict about gift orders, so the FDE asks the Customer Care lead, who picks one and updates the SOP.
subtopics.code:
ROLE
You are the support assistant for Brindlecove Home, an online homeware shop.
You help with order status, returns and refunds. Nothing else.

RULES (from SOP-RET v7, owner: Customer Care lead)
1. Verify the customer first: order number AND the email on the order.
   Never reveal order details before verification succeeds.
2. Returns: items can be returned within 30 days of delivery.
   Explain this rule before starting a return.
3. Refunds: use the issue_refund tool. Never promise a refund the tool
   has not confirmed. If the tool says needs_human, say a colleague will
   review it within 1 working day.
4. Damaged items: ask for a photo, then hand off to a human with
   reason "damaged_item". Do not argue about damage.
5. Hand off immediately if the customer asks for a person, is upset
   after two replies, or mentions a legal claim, injury or fraud.

STYLE
Short, friendly, plain sentences. One question at a time.
If you do not know, say so and offer a handoff. Never invent a policy.

rows: Order must belong to the customer

subtopics.title: Knowledge sources and actions
subtopics.body:
An agent has two kinds of capability. Knowledge lets it answer questions: help-centre articles, policy pages and product data, usually searched with retrieval as in the RAG topic. Actions let it change or read live data through tools: lookup_order, start_return, issue_refund, update_address.

For knowledge, pick the sources the support team trusts, remove outdated articles, and record each article's owner and last review date. Stale knowledge is the most common cause of confident wrong answers. Ask the agent to answer only from retrieved content and to say it does not know otherwise.

For actions, start read-only (look up an order) and add write actions one at a time. Each write tool should: take the verified customer ID from the session, never from the model's text; check every business rule itself; return a clear status such as refunded, needs_human or refused with a reason; and log the call. The model chooses when to call a tool, but the tool decides what is allowed. That is the idea of least privilege from the Guardrails topic applied to money and personal data.

Edge cases: partial refunds, orders split across shipments, a customer with two accounts, and the order system being down. For the last one the tool should return an error status and the agent should apologise and hand off, never guess.
subtopics.example: At Brindlecove the agent can call lookup_order and issue_refund. A customer asks for a 420 refund on order T-10501. The model calls issue_refund; the tool sees the amount is over the 150 auto-approve limit and returns needs_human. The agent tells the customer a colleague will review it within one working day and creates a ticket. A second customer tries to get a refund on an order that belongs to someone else; the tool refuses because the order's customer does not match the verified session.

subtopics.title: Handoff to a human with full context
subtopics.body:
A handoff (also called escalation or transfer) moves the conversation from the agent to a human agent. Customers forgive a handoff; they do not forgive repeating their story. So the handoff is a product feature you design, not a failure path.

Decide the triggers first: the customer asks for a person; a rule requires it (damage, injury, legal words, fraud); a tool returns needs_human; the agent has failed to make progress after two or three turns; or sentiment turns angry. Put hard triggers in code where possible, for example a keyword and classifier check, so they fire even if the model misses them.

Then design the package the human receives: the right queue, a priority, the verified identity, a two or three sentence summary, what the agent already tried and the result of each tool call, and a link to the transcript. Most helpdesk platforms (Zendesk, Salesforce Service Cloud, Intercom and others) let you create a ticket or transfer a chat with fields and internal notes through their API.

Finally, handle the waiting time. Tell the customer honestly what happens next and how long it usually takes. Outside staffed hours, the agent should create a ticket and promise a reply time instead of transferring into an empty queue.
subtopics.example: A Brindlecove customer writes that a lamp arrived cracked and they are furious. The damage rule fires, so the agent asks for a photo, then hands off. The human in the returns queue sees: verified customer c-881, order T-10442, 'Lamp arrived with cracked base, photo attached', lookup_order already done, priority high. The human sends a replacement in one reply instead of asking four questions.
subtopics.code:
import json

def build_handoff(conv):
    """Package everything a human agent needs so the customer never repeats themselves."""
    return {
        "queue": "returns_l2" if conv["reason"] == "damaged_item" else "general_l1",
        "priority": "high" if conv["sentiment"] == "angry" else "normal",
        "customer": {"id": conv["customer_id"], "verified": conv["verified"]},
        "reason": conv["reason"],
        "summary": conv["summary"],               # 2-3 sentences written by the agent
        "tried": conv["actions"],                 # tool calls and their results
        "transcript_url": f"https://support.example/t/{conv['id']}",
    }

conv = {"id": "cv-5521", "customer_id": "c-881", "verified": True,
        "reason": "damaged_item", "sentiment": "angry",
        "summary": "Lamp from order T-10442 arrived with a cracked base. Photo received.",
        "actions": [{"tool": "lookup_order", "result": "delivered 2 Sep"}]}
h = build_handoff(conv)
print(h["queue"], h["priority"])
print(json.dumps(h["tried"]))
# Output:
# returns_l2 high
# [{"tool": "lookup_order", "result": "delivered 2 Sep"}]
checklist: Handoff triggers listed and at least the hard ones enforced in code
Summary, verified identity and tool results passed to the human
Correct queue and priority chosen automatically
Customer told what happens next and how long it takes
After-hours path creates a ticket instead of a dead transfer

subtopics.title: Simulated conversations and regression tests
subtopics.body:
You cannot test an agent by chatting with it a few times. You need a test set of conversations with the outcome the SOP requires, run automatically on every change to the prompt, tools, knowledge or model. This is the Evals topic applied to dialogue.

Build the set from three places. Real transcripts from the human team, with personal data removed, give you realistic wording. SOP rules give you one case per rule, including the edges (day 30 versus day 31 of the return window). Red-team cases try to break policy: "my manager already approved a full refund", or instructions hidden in a pasted message.

For each case record the expected outcome, not the exact words: resolved with an order status, refund tool called with the right amount, handoff with reason damaged_item, or refused. Single-turn cases check routing. Multi-turn cases use a simulated customer, often another LLM given a persona and a goal ("you are an impatient customer who wants a refund for a late delivery"), and a judge that checks the outcome and policy compliance with a rubric.

Run the suite before every release and block the release if a previously passing case fails. Track the pass rate per intent, because an overall 95 percent can hide a 60 percent score on refunds.
subtopics.example: Brindlecove's suite starts with 60 cases: 30 from transcripts, 20 from SOP rules and 10 red-team. A prompt change that made replies friendlier also made the agent start refunds before explaining the 30-day window; three SOP cases failed and the change was fixed before release. The code below shows the harness shape with a rules-based stand-in for the real agent.
subtopics.code:
# A tiny stand-in for the real agent so the test harness can run offline.
def mock_agent(message, verified=True):
    m = message.lower()
    if not verified:
        return "ask_verification"
    if any(w in m for w in ["human", "person", "lawyer", "injur"]):
        return "handoff"
    if "broken" in m or "cracked" in m or "damaged" in m:
        return "handoff"
    if "refund" in m or "return" in m:
        return "refund_flow"
    if "where is" in m or "track" in m:
        return "order_status"
    return "clarify"

# Each case: customer message, verified?, the outcome the SOP requires
CASES = [
    ("Where is my order T-10442?",                 True,  "order_status"),
    ("I want a refund for the rug",                True,  "refund_flow"),
    ("The lamp arrived cracked",                   True,  "handoff"),
    ("Let me talk to a real person",               True,  "handoff"),
    ("Refund order T-10501 now",                   False, "ask_verification"),
    ("My kettle burned my hand, I was injured",   True,  "handoff"),
]
passed = 0
for msg, ver, expected in CASES:
    got = mock_agent(msg, ver)
    ok = got == expected
    passed += ok
    if not ok:
        print("FAIL:", msg, "->", got, "expected", expected)
print(f"{passed}/{len(CASES)} passed")
# Output:
# 6/6 passed

subtopics.title: Metrics: containment, resolution, CSAT, escalation
subtopics.body:
Four numbers tell you whether the agent works. Containment rate is the share of conversations that ended without a human. Escalation rate is the share handed to a human, so the two add up to 100 percent when every conversation ends one of those two ways. Resolution rate is the share where the problem was actually solved; a common proxy is 'no recontact about the same issue within 7 days'. CSAT (customer satisfaction) usually comes from a one-question survey after the conversation, reported as the share of 4 or 5 ratings on a 1 to 5 scale.

Containment on its own is dangerous. A customer who gives up and closes the chat counts as contained. So always report resolution of contained conversations beside it, plus recontact and abandonment. Also watch average handling time for the human team: good handoffs should make their conversations shorter.

Slice every metric by intent (order status, returns, damage), by channel and by new versus returning customers. Survey response rates are low and skewed toward unhappy customers, so read transcripts too: a weekly sample of 50, scored against a rubric, catches problems numbers miss.

Agree on the baseline before launch: the current cost per conversation, resolution and CSAT for the human team. Value is measured against that baseline, as in the ROI topic.
subtopics.example: In the code below 7 of 10 conversations stayed with the agent, so containment is 70 percent. But only 4 of those 7 were resolved without the customer coming back, so resolution of contained conversations is 57 percent. That gap is where the FDE looks first.
subtopics.code:
# One row per conversation from last week's logs
convs = [
    # (handled_by, resolved, recontact_7d, csat 1-5 or None)
    ("agent", True,  False, 5), ("agent", True,  False, 4), ("agent", False, True, 2),
    ("agent", True,  True,  3), ("agent", True,  False, None), ("human", True, False, 5),
    ("agent", False, True,  1), ("human", True,  False, 4), ("agent", True, False, 5),
    ("human", False, True,  2),
]
n = len(convs)
contained = [c for c in convs if c[0] == "agent"]
containment = len(contained) / n
escalation = 1 - containment
# Truly resolved: resolved AND the customer did not come back within 7 days
true_res = sum(1 for c in contained if c[1] and not c[2]) / len(contained)
rated = [c[3] for c in convs if c[3] is not None]
csat = sum(1 for r in rated if r >= 4) / len(rated)
print(f"containment {containment:.0%}, escalation {escalation:.0%}")
print(f"resolution of contained {true_res:.0%}, CSAT {csat:.0%}")
# Output:
# containment 70%, escalation 30%
# resolution of contained 57%, CSAT 56%

subtopics.title: Launch: shadow mode, percentage rollout, review
subtopics.body:
Launch in stages so a mistake reaches few customers. Stage one is shadow mode: the agent reads real incoming conversations and drafts a reply, but only human agents see it. They send their own reply and mark whether the draft was usable. This measures quality on real traffic with zero customer risk and trains the team to trust the agent.

Stage two is a percentage rollout: a small share of real conversations, often 5 percent, goes to the agent. Choose customers with a stable hash of their ID, so the same customer does not bounce between agent and human, and so widening from 5 to 25 percent keeps the first group in. Limit early rollout by intent too, for example order status only.

Stage three is review and widen. Each day, review a sample of transcripts and every escalation and complaint. Widen only when agreed thresholds hold for a week, for example resolution at or above the human baseline and zero policy violations. Keep a kill switch, a flag that sends all traffic back to humans in one step, and make sure the support lead knows how to use it.

After full launch the loop continues: new failure transcripts become new test cases, and SOP changes trigger prompt and tool updates with the suite as the gate.
subtopics.example: Brindlecove ran shadow mode for 2 weeks; human agents rated 81 percent of drafts usable, and the misses clustered on gift orders, which were fixed. The agent then took 5 percent of order-status and returns chats, then 25 percent, then 100 percent over five weeks, with a daily 20-minute transcript review between the FDE and the Customer Care lead.
subtopics.code:
import hashlib

def in_rollout(customer_id, percent, salt="agent-v2"):
    """Stable bucketing: the same customer always gets the same answer."""
    h = int(hashlib.sha256(f"{salt}:{customer_id}".encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
    return h % 100 < percent

customers = [f"c-{i}" for i in range(1000)]
for pct in (5, 25, 50):
    share = sum(in_rollout(c, pct) for c in customers) / len(customers)
    print(f"{pct}% target -> {share:.1%} of 1,000 customers")
# Anyone in the 5% group stays in the 25% group when you widen it
five = {c for c in customers if in_rollout(c, 5)}
print(all(in_rollout(c, 25) for c in five))
# Output:
# 5% target -> 5.9% of 1,000 customers
# 25% target -> 24.9% of 1,000 customers
# 50% target -> 51.0% of 1,000 customers
# True

glossary: SOP
Standard operating procedure: the written steps a support team follows for a type of request.
Macro
A saved reply template a human support agent inserts, often a good source of approved wording.
Action tool
A function the agent may call to read or change live data, such as lookup_order or issue_refund.
Handoff
Moving a conversation from the AI agent to a human agent, ideally with a summary and context.
Containment rate
Share of conversations that ended without a human joining.
Resolution rate
Share of conversations where the problem was solved, often measured as no recontact within 7 days.
CSAT
Customer satisfaction score from a short survey, often the share of 4 and 5 ratings on a 1 to 5 scale.
Recontact
The same customer coming back about the same issue within a set window, a sign it was not resolved.
Shadow mode
Running the agent on real traffic where only staff see its drafts, so quality is measured with no customer risk.
Kill switch
A flag that sends all conversations back to humans in one step.
practice: Take a one-page returns policy (write one if needed) and sort every rule into prompt instruction, tool check or handoff trigger in a three-column table.
Extend the issue_refund function with a rule that gift orders can only be refunded to the gift giver, and add three test calls that prove it.
Write 12 simulated test cases for an order-status and returns agent, including 3 red-team cases, each with an expected outcome, and run them against the mock agent.

Given a week of logs with 400 conversations, 290 handled by the agent, 60 of those with recontact, compute containment and resolution of contained conversations and write two sentences for the support lead.
Stretch: write a one-page launch plan with shadow, 5 percent and 25 percent stages, the exit threshold for each and who can pull the kill switch.

expansion.plain: Most software sold to businesses is paid for by subscription and renewed each year. Renewal is the customer deciding to keep paying; expansion is the customer buying more, for example more users or a second use case. Value realisation means showing, with real numbers, the benefit the customer actually got compared with where they started (the baseline). After go-live, a customer success manager (CSM) usually owns the relationship, and the FDE supplies the technical health, the value numbers and the ideas for what to build next.
expansion.analogy: It is like a gym membership. People renew when they can see the results they joined for. A good coach writes down your starting weight and goal on day one, notices when you stop coming, and suggests the next goal once the first one is reached.
expansion.why: An AI deployment that works but whose value nobody can state is at risk at renewal time, because a new CFO sees only a cost. FDEs are often the people closest to the system and its users, so they notice falling usage, a departing champion or a team next door with the same problem. Companies that sell through FDEs grow mainly through these second and third use cases, which is the Net Revenue Retention idea from the Sales-led growth topic.

subtopics.title: Customer success versus FDE after go-live
subtopics.body:
Once a system is live, several people share the account, and trouble starts when nobody knows who owns what. The customer success manager (CSM) owns the relationship after go-live: adoption, the success plan, health tracking and the renewal conversation. The account executive (AE) owns commercial terms: pricing, the contract and signing an expansion. Support owns tickets day to day, as described in the Support topic. The FDE owns the technical side: system health, fixes that need engineering, the value numbers pulled from logs, and the feasibility and first build of the next use case.

In smaller companies one person may cover two roles. That is fine as long as the list of responsibilities is written down and each item has one owner. A useful habit is a monthly 30-minute account sync between the CSM, AE and FDE where you review the health score, open risks and expansion ideas.

On the customer side, map the same roles: the executive sponsor who funds it, the business owner who runs the process, the champion who pushes adoption and the IT owner who runs the system after handoff. When any of these people change, the account is at risk until the replacement is onboarded.

A frequent edge case is the FDE being pulled onto a new customer right after go-live. Agree before go-live how many hours per month the FDE keeps for the account and for how long.
subtopics.example: At a freight company live on an invoice assistant, the CSM runs a monthly adoption review with the AP manager, the FDE produces the minutes-per-invoice numbers from logs and fixes a slow carrier mapping, and the AE prepares the renewal quote. When the AP manager mentions the payments team gets 400 'where is my payment' emails a week, the FDE writes a one-page feasibility note and the CSM takes it to the sponsor.

subtopics.title: The success plan and value realised
subtopics.body:
A success plan is a short shared document that lists the customer's goals, how each is measured, the baseline, the target and the date, plus the milestones and owners on both sides. It is written with the sponsor at kickoff and reviewed every month or quarter. The Success plan template in the Templates section gives the full shape.

Value realised is the benefit the customer actually received so far. To compute it you need the same measurement as the baseline, taken the same way. If the baseline was 7 minutes per invoice from a time study, measure minutes per invoice again, ideally from system logs so the number is repeatable. Convert to money only with a rate the customer's finance team gives you, such as a loaded cost per hour (salary plus benefits and overhead).

Report three numbers: realised to date, the current run rate (the latest month multiplied by 12) and the target from the plan. Be honest about attribution: if volume rose or a process changed at the same time, say so. Leading indicators such as weekly active users and share of work going through the system tell you whether the lagging business outcome will arrive.

Edge cases: goals nobody can measure (rewrite them early), baselines never captured (take one now on the teams not yet using the system), and targets that were sales promises, which you should reset openly with the sponsor.
subtopics.example: In the code below the baseline was 7 minutes per invoice and the finance team's loaded cost is 38 dollars per hour. Three months after go-live the assistant has saved about 5,500 clerk hours, worth about 208,500 dollars, and the latest month's run rate is about double the value committed in the success plan. The FDE shares this with the AP manager and finance before any executive sees it.
subtopics.code:
# Value tracker: same measure as the baseline, from system logs
baseline_min_per_item = 7.0      # measured in discovery, before go-live
loaded_cost_per_hour = 38.0      # finance's number for one clerk hour
months = {                       # month: (items processed, avg minutes per item)
    "Jul": (30500, 4.1), "Aug": (31800, 3.4), "Sep": (32400, 3.1),
}
committed_annual = 480000        # value target in the success plan

realised = 0
for m, (items, mins) in months.items():
    saved_hours = items * (baseline_min_per_item - mins) / 60
    value = saved_hours * loaded_cost_per_hour
    realised += value
    print(f"{m}: {saved_hours:,.0f} hours saved, ${value:,.0f}")
run_rate = value * 12            # annualise the latest month
print(f"Realised so far ${realised:,.0f}; run rate ${run_rate:,.0f} "
      f"= {run_rate / committed_annual:.0%} of the committed annual value")
# Output:
# Jul: 1,474 hours saved, $56,018
# Aug: 1,908 hours saved, $72,504
# Sep: 2,106 hours saved, $80,028
# Realised so far $208,550; run rate $960,336 = 200% of the committed annual value

subtopics.title: Renewal risk signals and saving an account
subtopics.body:
Accounts rarely churn (cancel) by surprise. The signals appear months earlier, and your job is to see them while there is still time. Usage signals: weekly active users or volume falling for several weeks, one team stopping entirely, users working around the system. People signals: the champion or sponsor leaving or changing role, no executive contact in a quarter, a new leader who did not choose you. Quality signals: open severity-1 or severity-2 tickets, repeated complaints about the same issue, falling accuracy. Commercial signals: budget cuts, a merger, a competitor being trialled, procurement asking unusual questions.

Many teams combine these into a health score, green, amber or red, with weights that are visible and argued about. The score is a prompt for action, never the answer. For each red or amber signal write a save plan: the cause, one action, an owner and a date.

Typical saves: fix the bug or workflow that made a team stop, onboard a new champion within two weeks of the old one leaving and brief their manager, run an executive business review to show value to a new leader, or trade scope, for example pausing an unused module to fund one that is working.

Start the renewal conversation at least 90 to 120 days before the renewal date, so there is time to fix what you find.
subtopics.example: Four months before renewal the health score for a logistics customer drops to red: weekly users down 22 percent, the AP manager who championed it has left, one severity-1 ticket about a new carrier format is open, and nobody has met an executive in 90 days. The FDE fixes the carrier format in a week, the CSM books the new AP manager for onboarding, and together they propose a 45-minute review with the CFO.
subtopics.code:
# A simple account health score. Weights are a team choice; keep them visible.
signals = {
    # name: (value, healthy_if, weight)
    "weekly_active_users_trend": (-0.22, lambda v: v >= -0.05, 30),  # -22% over 4 weeks
    "champion_still_in_role":    (False, lambda v: v, 25),
    "open_sev1_tickets":         (1,     lambda v: v == 0, 20),
    "exec_contact_last_90_days": (False, lambda v: v, 15),
    "value_reported_this_qtr":   (True,  lambda v: v, 10),
}
score = sum(w for v, ok, w in signals.values() if ok(v))
print("Health score:", score, "/ 100")
for name, (v, ok, w) in signals.items():
    if not ok(v):
        print(f"  RISK {name} = {v} (weight {w})")
status = "green" if score >= 75 else "amber" if score >= 50 else "red"
print("Status:", status)
# Output:
# Health score: 10 / 100
#   RISK weekly_active_users_trend = -0.22 (weight 30)
#   RISK champion_still_in_role = False (weight 25)
#   RISK open_sev1_tickets = 1 (weight 20)
#   RISK exec_contact_last_90_days = False (weight 15)
# Status: red
checklist: Usage trend checked weekly, by team, not only in total
Champion, sponsor and IT owner confirmed still in role each month
Open severity-1 and severity-2 tickets reviewed with the account team
Executive has seen value numbers in the last 90 days
Every amber or red signal has a save action, owner and date
Renewal conversation started 90 to 120 days before the date

subtopics.title: Finding the second use case
subtopics.body:
The easiest expansion is a second use case that reuses what the first one built: the same data, the same integration, the same users or the same approval path. It is cheaper to build, faster to prove and easier for the sponsor to approve, because the risk has already been retired once. This is the 'land and expand' pattern from the Sales-led growth topic.

Where to look: teams upstream or downstream of the first workflow, other regions or business units doing the same process, the exceptions queue of the first use case, and requests users make that are out of scope today. Keep a running list in the account plan from the first week; FDEs hear these ideas constantly on site.

Score each candidate on value (hours or money at stake), reuse (how much of the existing build applies), data readiness and sponsor interest. The scoring method is the same as in the AI readiness topic. Take only the top one or two to the sponsor, each with a rough value estimate, effort in weeks, what is reused and a small first step such as a 4 to 6 week pilot.

Edge cases: a use case that is valuable but belongs to a team that has no budget (find the sponsor before pitching), and requests that are really product features, which go to your product team instead.
subtopics.example: At the freight company the FDE's list has three ideas. A carrier payment-status agent reuses the same AP data and Ledgerline integration and would answer about 400 emails a week. Customs document extraction is valuable but needs new data and a new team. An HR chatbot has no link to the current work. The scoring below puts the payment-status agent first, and the sponsor approves a 6-week pilot.
subtopics.code:
# Score candidate second use cases 1-5 on each factor
candidates = {
    # name: (value, reuse of data and integration, data ready, sponsor keen)
    "Carrier payment-status agent (same AP data)": (4, 5, 4, 4),
    "Customs document extraction (new data)":     (5, 2, 2, 3),
    "HR policy chatbot (new team, new data)":     (2, 1, 3, 2),
}
weights = (0.35, 0.25, 0.2, 0.2)
ranked = sorted(candidates.items(),
                key=lambda kv: -sum(s * w for s, w in zip(kv[1], weights)))
for name, scores in ranked:
    total = sum(s * w for s, w in zip(scores, weights))
    print(f"{total:.2f}  {name}")
# Output:
# 4.25  Carrier payment-status agent (same AP data)
# 3.25  Customs document extraction (new data)
# 1.95  HR policy chatbot (new team, new data)

subtopics.title: The executive business review
subtopics.body:
An executive business review (EBR, also called a QBR when it is quarterly) is a meeting with the customer's sponsor and senior leaders to review the value delivered and decide what happens next. It is not a status report and not a product demo. Executives come to make a decision, so the whole meeting points at one clear ask.

Prepare the numbers with the customer's own owners first. If their finance lead has agreed the value figure, nobody in the room will argue with it. Send a short pre-read 5 working days before: the goals from the success plan, baseline and today for each, and the proposed next step.

In the room, lead with outcomes in their words, then value delivered, then a short quote from a real user. Include one honest section on what did not go well and what you changed; this builds more trust than a perfect story. Then the next six months and the ask: approve a pilot, name an owner, agree the renewal timeline. Close with actions, owners and dates, and send them in writing the same day.

Who does what: the CSM usually runs the EBR, the FDE presents the value numbers and the technical roadmap, and the AE handles any commercial questions. Keep it to 45 minutes and 8 to 10 slides. The Executive communication topic covers answer-first structure for the slides.
subtopics.example: For the freight company's review, the pre-read shows minutes per invoice down from 7.0 to 3.1 and about 208,000 dollars realised in three months, agreed by the finance controller. The FDE presents the payment-status agent idea with a value estimate of about 150,000 dollars a year. The CFO approves a 6-week pilot and names the payments team lead as owner.
subtopics.code:
EXECUTIVE BUSINESS REVIEW  (45 minutes, sponsor + 3-5 leaders)
Sent 5 working days before, with the numbers agreed by their finance lead

1. Outcomes we agreed (2 min)
   The three goals from the success plan, in their words.
2. Value delivered (10 min)
   Baseline -> today for each goal. One chart, one number per goal.
   Example: minutes per invoice 7.0 -> 3.1; $208k realised in 3 months.
3. What the users say (5 min)
   One short quote from a daily user, one from their manager.
4. What did not go well and what we did (5 min)
   Be specific. Executives trust a review that admits a miss.
5. Next 6 months (10 min)
   Roadmap items, adoption goals, and ONE proposed next use case
   with a rough value estimate.
6. The ask (5 min)
   A clear decision: approve a 6-week pilot for use case 2,
   name an owner, confirm renewal timeline.
7. Actions, owners, dates (3 min)

subtopics.title: Referencing: case studies and customer references
subtopics.body:
A reference is a happy customer who agrees to speak to a prospective customer. A case study is a short published story of the customer's problem, approach and results. Both help your company win the next deal, and both depend on the trust the FDE built on site.

Ask at the right moment: after the customer has seen and agreed value numbers, usually right after a good EBR, never during an incident or before renewal is settled. Ask the sponsor or champion, not their staff. Make it easy to say yes and easy to say no. Offer choices of different sizes: a single call per quarter, an anonymous written story, a quote, a joint conference talk.

The customer's legal and communications teams usually must approve any public use of their name or logo, and the contract may already say whether you can use it. Never share numbers or details the customer has not approved in writing. An anonymous case study ('a North American freight forwarder') is often approved much faster.

Protect your references. Track how often each one is used, do not send them more than about one call a quarter, brief them before each call on who the prospect is, and thank them afterwards. A tired reference soon stops saying yes.
subtopics.example: After the review, the FDE drafts the note below to the CFO offering two options. The CFO agrees to an anonymous written case study. The FDE writes a 400-word draft using only the numbers from the pre-read, the customer's communications team edits two sentences, and legal approves it in three weeks.
subtopics.code:
Subject: Would you share the invoice results with one peer company?

Hi Dana,

Thank you again for Tuesday's review. Your team's result, invoice
handling time down from 7 minutes to about 3, has been the clearest
proof we have that this approach works in freight.

Would you be open to one of these, whichever suits you best?
  1. A 20-minute call with one prospective customer, at most once a
     quarter, scheduled around you.
  2. A short written case study. You approve every word before it
     is shared, and we can leave the company name out.

No is a perfectly fine answer and changes nothing about our work.

Best regards,
Priya
checklist: Value numbers agreed by the customer before you ask
Ask the sponsor or champion after a good review, not during trouble
Offer options: one call, anonymous story, quote, joint talk
Customer legal and communications approve the final wording
Log each reference call and brief the reference beforehand

glossary: Renewal
The customer choosing to continue a subscription contract for another term.
Expansion
The customer buying more: more users, more volume or a new use case.
Churn
A customer cancelling or not renewing.
Customer success manager (CSM)
The person who owns the customer relationship, adoption and renewal after go-live.
Success plan
A shared document listing the customer's goals, measures, baselines, targets, milestones and owners.
Value realised
The measured benefit the customer has actually received so far, compared with the baseline.
Run rate
The latest period's result scaled to a year, for example the last month multiplied by 12.
Health score
A combined green, amber or red rating of an account from usage, people, quality and commercial signals.
Executive business review (EBR)
A meeting with the customer's leaders to review value delivered and decide next steps.
Customer reference
A customer who agrees to talk to prospective customers about their experience.
practice: Write a one-page success plan for an invented customer with three goals, each with a measure, baseline, target and date.
Change the value tracker so it also reports value per month as a share of the monthly target, and flag any month under 80 percent.
Add two more signals to the health score (for example 'competitor trial' and 'ticket volume trend'), rebalance the weights and explain your choice in two sentences.
List five places you would look for a second use case at a hospital that uses an AI discharge-summary assistant, and score the top three.
Stretch: draft the pre-read and 8-slide outline for an executive business review where one goal was met and one was missed.

psa.plain: Professional services is paid work done for a customer by people, such as setting up, integrating and training, as opposed to the software licence itself. Services operations is how that work is priced, staffed, tracked and billed. PSA, professional services automation, is software that runs it: project plans, resourcing (who works on what and when), time tracking, billing and a portal the customer can see. The Last-mile onboarding topic introduced playbooks and portals; this topic explains the business behind them.
psa.analogy: Think of a building contractor. They can charge by the hour, quote a fixed price for the whole kitchen, or bill at stages. They need to know which workers are free next week, whether this job is eating more hours than the quote, and a shared plan so the homeowner knows when the plumber arrives. A PSA tool is their office.
psa.why: FDE teams are often measured partly as a services business: did the project hit its budget, how many hours were billable, is delivery getting cheaper with each customer. An FDE who agrees a fixed price on unknown scope can turn a good deployment into a loss. Understanding these numbers lets you scope honestly, raise change requests at the right time and build the reusable playbooks that make the next deployment faster.

subtopics.title: Services models: T&M, fixed fee, milestones, retainers
subtopics.body:
The pricing model in the statement of work (SOW) decides how hours turn into money and who carries the risk if the work takes longer.

Time and materials (T&M): the customer pays for the hours actually worked at an agreed rate, plus expenses. The customer carries the overrun risk, so it suits unclear scope such as discovery. Many customers ask for a not-to-exceed cap, which moves risk back to you above the cap.

Fixed fee: one price for a defined scope. Your company carries the risk; if it takes longer, margin falls. It suits well-understood, repeated work. The protection is a tight scope, written assumptions (for example 'customer provides API access by week 2') and a change-request process.

Milestones: payment tied to accepted deliverables, such as 30 percent at design sign-off. It is usually fixed fee split into stages, and it makes acceptance criteria very important.

Retainer: a fixed monthly fee for a block of hours or ongoing access, common for support after go-live. Say what happens to unused hours.

Outcome-based: payment linked to a business result, such as cost per resolved ticket. It aligns incentives but needs a baseline and a measurement both sides trust, and outcomes you actually control.

Many deals mix them: T&M discovery, then a fixed-fee build with milestones, then a retainer.
subtopics.example: A logistics customer wants an invoice assistant. The vendor proposes 3 weeks of T&M discovery at 250 per hour to probe the ERP API, then a 100,000 fixed-fee build paid at design sign-off, pilot acceptance and go-live, then a 6,000 per month support retainer covering 20 hours. The customer gets price certainty for the build once the biggest unknown is gone.

subtopics.title: Utilisation, margin and why they matter
subtopics.body:
Utilisation is the share of a person's available hours that were billable to a customer. If someone has 160 hours available in a month and 120 were billable, utilisation is 75 percent. Services leaders track it by person, team and month, because unbilled hours are paid for by the company.

Margin is what is left after delivery costs, as a share of revenue: (revenue minus cost) divided by revenue. Delivery cost is mainly the loaded cost of the people's hours: salary, benefits, taxes and overhead per hour. Project margin compares one project's revenue with the hours it actually used. Services teams at software companies often run at much lower margins than software licences, and some deliberately run services near break-even to win and keep the software revenue.

Why an FDE cares: an overrun on a fixed-fee project comes straight out of margin, and hours spent on rework or unpaid scope creep lower utilisation. That is why raising a change request early matters.

Edge case: 100 percent utilisation is not the goal. People need time for training, internal tools, helping sales and building reusable connectors, which make future projects cheaper. Many teams target somewhere around 65 to 80 percent for delivery staff, and less for leads. Low utilisation for a week is fine when the time went into reuse.
subtopics.example: The code shows one 400-hour project with a 25 percent overrun, a rate of 250 per hour and a loaded cost of 110 per hour. Under T&M the customer pays for all 500 hours and margin stays at 56 percent. With a 440-hour cap it falls to 50 percent, and as a 100,000 fixed fee it falls to 45 percent. The second block shows a team's utilisation: Dara is at 38 percent because she spent two weeks building a reusable connector, which is a good reason.
subtopics.code:
def project_margin(model, rate, planned_hours, overrun_pct, cost_per_hour,
                   fee=None, cap_hours=None):
    actual = planned_hours * (1 + overrun_pct / 100)
    if model == "t&m":                       # customer pays every hour
        revenue = actual * rate
    elif model == "t&m_capped":              # pays up to a not-to-exceed cap
        revenue = min(actual, cap_hours) * rate
    elif model == "fixed":                   # one price, whatever it takes
        revenue = fee
    cost = actual * cost_per_hour
    return revenue, cost, (revenue - cost) / revenue

# Same project, 400 planned hours, 25% overrun, 250/h rate, 110/h cost
for model, kw in [("t&m", {}), ("t&m_capped", {"cap_hours": 440}),
                  ("fixed", {"fee": 100000})]:
    rev, cost, m = project_margin(model, 250, 400, 25, 110, **kw)
    print(f"{model:11} revenue {rev:>8,.0f}  cost {cost:>7,.0f}  margin {m:.0%}")
# Output:
# t&m         revenue  125,000  cost  55,000  margin 56%
# t&m_capped  revenue  110,000  cost  55,000  margin 50%
# fixed       revenue  100,000  cost  55,000  margin 45%

# Four weeks for a 5-person delivery team, 40 available hours each per week
team = {  # name: (billable hours, non-billable project hours, internal hours)
    "Ana":   (128, 12, 20),
    "Ben":   (96,  30, 34),
    "Chidi": (140, 8,  12),
    "Dara":  (60,  20, 80),   # spent two weeks building a reusable connector
    "Eli":   (118, 22, 20),
}
available = 160
for name, (bill, nonbill, internal) in team.items():
    print(f"{name:6} utilisation {bill / available:.0%}")
total_bill = sum(b for b, _, _ in team.values())
print(f"Team   utilisation {total_bill / (available * len(team)):.0%}")
# Output:
# Ana    utilisation 80%
# Ben    utilisation 60%
# Chidi  utilisation 88%
# Dara   utilisation 38%
# Eli    utilisation 74%
# Team   utilisation 68%

subtopics.title: PSA platforms: one workspace and resourcing
subtopics.body:
Without a PSA platform, delivery lives in many places: the plan in a spreadsheet, time in another tool, the customer's tasks in email and invoices in finance software. PSA platforms join these into one workspace. Common features: project plans built from templates, resource management (skills, availability and bookings), time tracking with billable flags, budgets against actuals, billing rules per pricing model, a customer-facing portal, and reports on utilisation and margin. Most integrate with the CRM, so a signed deal can create the project automatically.

The market includes general PSA suites such as Kantata and Certinia, and tools focused on customer onboarding and implementation such as Rocketlane, which emphasises shared customer workspaces, templates and portals. Feature sets change quickly, so compare on your own needs rather than a list.

Resourcing is the part FDEs feel most. It compares demand (hours needed per role per week, from signed and likely projects) with capacity (bookable hours per person). Gaps show weeks ahead that two go-lives will collide or that data engineering is the bottleneck. Good resourcing uses soft bookings for likely deals and firm bookings for signed ones.

Edge cases: people split across many projects lose time switching; public holidays and planned leave must be in capacity; and a new tool will not fix a process nobody follows.
subtopics.example: A services lead sees in the resourcing view that week 42 has two go-lives. FDE demand is 185 hours against 160 available, and data engineering is short from week 41. She moves one go-live by a week with the customer's agreement and books a contractor data engineer for two weeks, instead of finding out in week 42.
subtopics.code:
# Weekly demand (hours) from signed and likely projects vs team capacity
capacity = {"FDE": 5 * 32, "Data engineer": 2 * 32}   # 32 bookable h/person/week
demand = {
    "W40": {"FDE": 120, "Data engineer": 50},
    "W41": {"FDE": 150, "Data engineer": 80},
    "W42": {"FDE": 185, "Data engineer": 70},   # two go-lives in one week
}
for week, need in demand.items():
    for role, hours in need.items():
        gap = capacity[role] - hours
        flag = "OVER" if gap < 0 else "ok"
        print(f"{week} {role:13} need {hours:3}  have {capacity[role]:3}  {flag}")
# Output:
# W40 FDE           need 120  have 160  ok
# W40 Data engineer need  50  have  64  ok
# W41 FDE           need 150  have 160  ok
# W41 Data engineer need  80  have  64  OVER
# W42 FDE           need 185  have 160  OVER
# W42 Data engineer need  70  have  64  OVER

subtopics.title: Dynamic playbooks and project templates
subtopics.body:
A playbook is the standard plan for a type of project: phases, tasks, typical durations, owners, documents and the checks at each gate. A dynamic playbook adds conditions, so tasks switch on or off based on facts about the customer: uses single sign-on or not, needs a historical backfill or not, is in a regulated industry or not. The Last-mile onboarding topic showed why reusable fixes matter; the playbook is where they are stored.

Build the first playbook from two or three finished projects. List every task that actually happened, including the surprises, with the real hours. Group them into phases that match your gates, for example kickoff, access, data, build, UAT and go-live. Attach templates to tasks: the SOW, the data inventory, UAT scripts, the runbook.

Then keep it alive. After each project, compare planned and actual hours per phase in the margin review, and change the estimates and tasks that were wrong. Record who owns the playbook and its version.

Edge cases: too many conditions make the playbook hard to read; keep it to the facts that really change the work. A playbook is a starting point; the FDE still adjusts the plan to the customer, and the SOW must match the plan, not an older version.
subtopics.example: A document-AI vendor's playbook has 8 core tasks and 3 conditional ones. For a customer with SSO, no document store and a backfill, the plan below starts with 36 effort days, and the SOW's fixed fee is priced from that number instead of a guess.
subtopics.code:
PLAYBOOK = [  # (phase, task, days, condition on customer facts or None)
    ("Kickoff",   "Kickoff call and success plan",        2, None),
    ("Access",    "Service account and network allowlist", 3, None),
    ("Access",    "SSO setup with the customer IdP",       3, lambda c: c["sso"]),
    ("Data",      "Connect document store",                4, lambda c: c["docstore"]),
    ("Data",      "Historical backfill and reconciliation", 5, lambda c: c["backfill"]),
    ("Build",     "Configure extraction and validation",   8, None),
    ("UAT",       "UAT scripts and sign-off",              5, None),
    ("Go-live",   "Cutover and hypercare",                 10, None),
]

def build_plan(customer):
    plan = [(p, t, d) for p, t, d, cond in PLAYBOOK if cond is None or cond(customer)]
    return plan, sum(d for _, _, d in plan)

facts = {"sso": True, "docstore": False, "backfill": True}
plan, days = build_plan(facts)
for phase, task, d in plan:
    print(f"{phase:8} {task} ({d}d)")
print("Total effort days:", days)
# Output:
# Kickoff  Kickoff call and success plan (2d)
# Access   Service account and network allowlist (3d)
# Access   SSO setup with the customer IdP (3d)
# Data     Historical backfill and reconciliation (5d)
# Build    Configure extraction and validation (8d)
# UAT      UAT scripts and sign-off (5d)
# Go-live  Cutover and hypercare (10d)
# Total effort days: 36

subtopics.title: Client portals and shared plans
subtopics.body:
A client portal is a web page, usually part of the PSA tool, where the customer sees the live project: phases and dates, what is blocked, their own open tasks with due dates, shared files and the next meeting. It replaces the status spreadsheet sent by email that is out of date the moment it is sent.

The biggest benefit is making customer-side work visible. Many delays in AI deployments are on the customer's side: an API key, a firewall change, sample data, testers for UAT. When those tasks have a named owner and a date in a place their manager can see, they get done faster, and nobody argues later about why the date moved.

Decide what the customer sees. Internal notes, margin, rates and your own team's risk discussion stay internal. Customer-facing tasks should be written in their language, not your ticket codes. Keep one plan: if the portal and your internal plan differ, the customer will eventually find out.

Use the portal to run the weekly check-in: walk through blocked items and their tasks first, then progress. Edge cases: customers who never log in (send a short weekly digest that links to it), and sensitive files that should stay in the customer's own systems rather than be uploaded.
subtopics.example: Harlow Freight's portal shows Access as blocked on a VPN allowlist that has waited 5 days on their IT lead. The AP manager sees it before the check-in and chases IT herself; the change is approved the next day, and the data phase keeps its date.
subtopics.code:
CLIENT PORTAL  Harlow Freight onboarding     (updated daily by the FDE)

Phase          Status        Target     Owner
Kickoff        Done          2 Sep      Both
Access         Blocked       9 Sep      HARLOW: IT lead
  - VPN allowlist for 2 IPs    waiting on customer since 4 Sep
Data           Not started   20 Sep     Vendor: FDE
Build          Not started   4 Oct      Vendor: FDE
UAT            Not started   14 Oct     HARLOW: AP manager

Your open tasks (3)
  [ ] Approve VPN allowlist request CHG-2291          due 9 Sep
  [ ] Share 200 sample invoices in the shared folder  due 12 Sep

checklist: Phases, dates and status match the internal plan
Every customer task has a named owner and a due date
Blocked items say what they are waiting for and since when
Rates, margin and internal notes are hidden from the customer
A weekly digest goes to people who do not log in

subtopics.title: AI automation inside services work
subtopics.body:
Services teams spend a lot of time on delivery paperwork: status updates, meeting notes, time entries, risk reports and handover documents. This is where AI helps most today, and where PSA tools have been adding AI features.

Useful automations: drafting the weekly status update from the plan, completed tasks and meeting notes; turning a call transcript into action items with owners; suggesting time entries from calendar events and commits for a person to confirm; generating a first project plan from the playbook and SOW; summarising a project for a new team member; and flagging projects at risk from simple signals such as budget burn ahead of progress, a customer that has gone quiet or unpriced change requests.

Keep a person in the loop for anything the customer sees or that affects billing. A status note that states a wrong date, or a time entry billed to the wrong customer, costs more trust than the time it saved. Also check where the data goes: meeting transcripts and plans may contain customer confidential information, so use tools covered by your company's agreements, as in the Security and Compliance topics.

Start with rules before models. The risk flags in the code are plain rules; an LLM can then write the explanation for the services lead to read. Measure the time saved on each task, just as you would for a customer.
subtopics.example: Every Monday a vendor's services lead gets a list of projects to review. Harlow is flagged because 62 percent of the budget is used with 40 percent of the work done and the customer has not replied for 9 days. Mornay is flagged for burn and two unpriced change requests. The lead calls both customers that day; the FDEs review AI-drafted status notes for the rest in minutes.
subtopics.code:
# Rules that flag projects for a human to look at, run every Monday
projects = [
    # name, % budget used, % work done, days since customer replied, open change requests
    ("Harlow onboarding",  62, 40, 9, 0),
    ("Selby claims pilot", 45, 50, 1, 0),
    ("Mornay data sync",   88, 70, 2, 2),
]
for name, budget, done, silent_days, crs in projects:
    reasons = []
    if budget - done >= 15:
        reasons.append(f"burn ahead of progress ({budget}% budget, {done}% done)")
    if silent_days >= 7:
        reasons.append(f"customer silent {silent_days} days")
    if crs:
        reasons.append(f"{crs} change requests not yet priced")
    print(("REVIEW " if reasons else "ok     ") + name + (": " + "; ".join(reasons) if reasons else ""))
# Output:
# REVIEW Harlow onboarding: burn ahead of progress (62% budget, 40% done); customer silent 9 days
# ok     Selby claims pilot
# REVIEW Mornay data sync: burn ahead of progress (88% budget, 70% done); 2 change requests not yet priced

glossary: Professional services
Paid work done by people for a customer, such as setup, integration and training.
PSA
Professional services automation: software for plans, resourcing, time, billing and client portals.
Time and materials (T&M)
Pricing where the customer pays for hours actually worked at an agreed rate.
Fixed fee
One agreed price for a defined scope, so the provider carries the overrun risk.
Not-to-exceed cap
A limit on the total T&M billing; hours above it are not paid.
Retainer
A fixed recurring fee for a block of hours or ongoing access.
Utilisation
Billable hours divided by available hours for a person or team.
Loaded cost
The full cost of one hour of a person's time: salary plus benefits, taxes and overhead.
Project margin
Project revenue minus delivery cost, divided by revenue.
Change request
A formal request to change scope, dates or price after the SOW is signed.
Resourcing
Matching people's skills and available hours to project demand over time.
practice: Using project_margin, find the overrun percentage at which the fixed-fee project's margin drops below 30 percent.
Write a one-paragraph pricing recommendation for a customer who wants a fixed price for an integration with an undocumented API.
Add a 'regulated industry' condition to the playbook that adds a DPIA task and a security review task, and show the new plan for one customer.
Sketch a client portal page for a 10-week deployment with at least 4 customer-side tasks, and mark what stays internal.
Stretch: add a rule to the risk flags for 'go-live within 14 days and UAT not signed', and test it on three invented projects.

lowcode.plain: Low-code platforms let people build software by dragging blocks, filling in forms and writing short formulas instead of writing whole programs. Many now include AI agent builders: you describe what the agent should do, give it knowledge (documents, websites) and actions (connectors to other systems), and publish it into a chat app or portal. Examples are Microsoft Copilot Studio, Salesforce Agentforce, ServiceNow's AI agents, n8n and Zapier. FDEs often build on these because the customer already owns and trusts them.
lowcode.analogy: Think of a flat-pack kitchen system. Most of the kitchen is assembled from standard units quickly, and anyone trained can later swap a door or add a shelf. When a corner does not fit any standard unit, a carpenter builds one custom piece that screws onto the same rails. The FDE is the carpenter who also knows the flat-pack system well.
lowcode.why: Large customers standardise on a few platforms and put them through security and compliance reviews once. A build on the approved platform can often go live in weeks instead of waiting months for a new security review of custom code, and the customer's own staff can maintain it. But low-code has limits, and an FDE who knows where they are can extend the platform with code in the right places instead of fighting it.

subtopics.title: The landscape: Copilot Studio, Agentforce, ServiceNow, n8n and Zapier
subtopics.body:
Low-code AI platforms fall into two families.

Suite platforms live inside a big business system and are strongest with that system's data and users. Microsoft Copilot Studio builds agents that publish to Teams, websites and Microsoft 365 Copilot. It uses Power Platform connectors and Power Automate flows as actions and can use SharePoint and other sources as knowledge. Salesforce Agentforce builds agents from topics (jobs the agent handles, with instructions) and actions (Flows, Apex code or prompt templates) grounded in the customer's CRM data. ServiceNow offers AI agents and Now Assist on top of its IT, HR and customer service workflows, with Flow Designer and IntegrationHub for connections.

Independent automation tools connect many apps. n8n is a workflow tool you can self-host (useful when data must stay inside the customer's network), with AI agent nodes, an HTTP Request node and a Code node for JavaScript or Python. Zapier is a cloud service with connectors for thousands of apps, webhooks, AI steps and agents; it is quick for small teams.

Key terms: a maker or citizen developer builds on the platform without being a professional developer; a connector is a prebuilt link to another system; a flow is an automated sequence of steps.

Edge case: features, names and pricing change quickly, often several times a year. Check the vendor's current documentation and the customer's licences before you promise a feature.
subtopics.example: An insurer with Microsoft 365 wants an internal HR agent in Teams, while its claims team works in Salesforce and wants a case-summary agent there. The FDE proposes Copilot Studio for the first and Agentforce for the second, rather than one custom app that both groups would need to open separately.

rows: Users live in Teams and Microsoft 365
Data and users are in Salesforce
IT, HR or service workflows run in ServiceNow
Data must stay on the customer's servers
You run and patch it if self-hosted
Small teams linking many SaaS apps fast
Data leaves to a cloud service, task costs

subtopics.title: When the customer's platform choice decides your build
subtopics.body:
In discovery, ask early: where do the users spend their day, where does the data live, what platforms has IT already approved, and is custom code allowed in production at all? The answers often choose the platform for you.

Reasons a customer's platform wins even if you could build something better in code: users already sign in there, so there is nothing new to install or learn; identity, permissions and audit logs are already set up; the security team has already reviewed it; the customer has licences they want to use; and their own staff can support it after you leave.

Reasons to push back: the platform cannot meet a hard requirement (for example a latency target or a data residency rule); the licence cost per user or per message would be far higher than the value; or the use case needs heavy custom logic that the customer's team could not maintain anyway. Put the trade-off in writing, with numbers, as in the Discovery and ROI topics.

The usual answer is a hybrid: the platform is the front door users see, and a small, well-tested API handles the hard part. This keeps the customer's governance happy and your logic testable.

Edge case: some customers have two suites (for example Microsoft 365 and Salesforce). Build where the task happens, and do not duplicate the same agent in both.
subtopics.example: The code is a rough first pass an FDE might sketch after a discovery call. It is not a rule, but it captures the main question: which platform already holds the users and the data, and does IT allow custom code?
subtopics.code:
# Rough first pass at where to build: which platform already holds the users and data?
def suggest(users_work_in, data_lives_in, it_allows_custom_code):
    home = {"Teams": "Copilot Studio", "Salesforce": "Agentforce",
            "ServiceNow portal": "ServiceNow AI agents"}
    if users_work_in in home and data_lives_in in (users_work_in, "same suite"):
        return home[users_work_in]
    if users_work_in in home and not it_allows_custom_code:
        return home[users_work_in] + " with a custom connector"
    if not it_allows_custom_code:
        return "n8n or Zapier, if IT approves the tool"
    return "custom code, if nothing above fits"

print(suggest("Teams", "same suite", False))
print(suggest("Salesforce", "Salesforce", True))
print(suggest("Teams", "old HR database", False))
print(suggest("email", "several SaaS apps", False))
# Output:
# Copilot Studio
# Agentforce
# Copilot Studio with a custom connector
# n8n or Zapier, if IT approves the tool

subtopics.title: Extending with custom connectors and APIs
subtopics.body:
Prebuilt connectors cover popular systems, but customers always have something unusual: an old HR database, an internal pricing service, your company's own product API. A custom connector lets the platform call it as if it were built in.

Most platforms describe a custom connector with an OpenAPI file (a YAML or JSON description of an API's paths, inputs, outputs and authentication). Power Platform custom connectors can be created from an OpenAPI definition; Salesforce External Services imports an OpenAPI schema and uses Named Credentials to store the login details; n8n and Zapier can call any API through an HTTP request step or a webhook.

Steps: 1) Build a small API that does one job well (see the FastAPI topic). 2) Write the OpenAPI file with a clear operationId and summary, because makers and the agent see those names. 3) Choose authentication the platform supports, such as an API key or OAuth 2.0. 4) Import it, test each action, and share the connection with the right people. 5) Version it: a breaking change to the API breaks every flow that uses it.

Design tips: keep inputs few and simple, return flat JSON with plain names, return helpful error messages, and keep responses fast, because platforms have request timeouts.

Edge case: if the API sits inside the customer's network, the cloud platform may need an on-premises data gateway or a secure tunnel to reach it; plan that with their network team early (see Enterprise networking).
subtopics.example: This is the OpenAPI file for a tiny leave-balance API that a Copilot Studio agent calls through a custom connector. After import, makers see one action named GetLeaveBalance with one input, employeeId, and the platform asks for the API key once when the connection is created.
subtopics.code:
openapi: 3.0.1
info:
  title: Leave Balance API
  version: "1.0"
servers:
  - url: https://leave-api.example.com
paths:
  /balance/{employeeId}:
    get:
      operationId: GetLeaveBalance        # the action name makers will see
      summary: Get remaining leave days for one employee
      parameters:
        - name: employeeId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema: {type: string}
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Remaining leave
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  employeeId: {type: string}
                  annualDaysLeft: {type: number}
                  asOf: {type: string, format: date}
components:
  securitySchemes:
    apiKey: {type: apiKey, in: header, name: X-API-Key}
security:
  - apiKey: []

subtopics.title: Governance: environments, DLP policies and who can publish
subtopics.body:
Because anyone can build on a low-code platform, customers control it with governance rules. Learn them in week one, not on launch day.

Environments: separate spaces for development, testing and production, each with its own data, connections and permissions. Build in dev, test in test, and move the finished work to production as a packaged unit (in Power Platform this is a solution, often moved by pipelines; Salesforce uses sandboxes and deployments). Never build directly in production.

Data loss prevention (DLP) policies: rules set by admins that sort connectors into groups. In Power Platform the groups are Business, Non-Business and Blocked. One app or flow cannot use connectors from both Business and Non-Business, and Blocked connectors cannot be used at all. A new custom connector may fall into the default group, which can break your flow in production even though it worked in dev.

Who can publish: many customers let anyone build in a personal or sandbox environment, but only approved makers or the Center of Excellence (see Enablement) can publish to everyone. Expect a review: what data the agent reads, what actions it can take, who owns it.

Also check: sharing limits on connections, audit logging, which AI features are switched on for the tenant, and data residency for AI processing (see Compliance).

Edge case: an agent that uses the builder's own connection acts with the builder's permissions for every user. Prefer connections where each user signs in as themselves when the data is personal.
subtopics.example: The code checks a flow against a simplified DLP policy before publishing. The leave-balance flow fails because the new custom connector is still in Non-Business while SharePoint is Business; the fix is asking the admin to classify the connector as Business, not rebuilding the flow.
subtopics.code:
# A DLP policy puts every connector into one group. A flow may not mix
# connectors from the Business and Non-Business groups, and Blocked ones
# cannot be used at all. This checks a flow before you try to publish it.
POLICY = {
    "SharePoint": "Business", "Dataverse": "Business",
    "Office 365 Outlook": "Business", "HR Leave API (custom)": "Non-Business",
    "Twitter": "Non-Business", "Dropbox": "Blocked",
}

def check_flow(name, connectors):
    groups = {POLICY.get(c, "Non-Business") for c in connectors}  # unlisted -> default group
    if "Blocked" in groups:
        bad = [c for c in connectors if POLICY.get(c) == "Blocked"]
        return f"{name}: FAIL, blocked connector {bad}"
    if {"Business", "Non-Business"} <= groups:
        return f"{name}: FAIL, mixes Business and Non-Business connectors"
    return f"{name}: ok ({groups.pop()})"

print(check_flow("Leave balance", ["SharePoint", "HR Leave API (custom)"]))
print(check_flow("Policy answer", ["SharePoint", "Dataverse"]))
print(check_flow("Export report", ["Office 365 Outlook", "Dropbox"]))
# Output:
# Leave balance: FAIL, mixes Business and Non-Business connectors
# Policy answer: ok (Business)
# Export report: FAIL, blocked connector ['Dropbox']

subtopics.title: Limits and when to drop to code
subtopics.body:
Low-code is fast for common patterns and slow for unusual ones. Know the limits you will hit.

Platform limits: request and run quotas per user or per day, timeouts on a single action, payload size limits, and throttling when many users arrive at once. Look these up in the vendor's current documentation for the customer's licence.

Engineering limits: complex business rules become huge visual flows that nobody can read; unit testing and code review are weak or missing; version control and diffs are harder; and heavy data work (thousands of rows, big files) is slow and expensive.

AI limits: you control less of the prompt, model choice and retrieval, so evaluation matters even more. Build a test set of real questions and check answers before and after every change, as in the Evals topic.

Cost: many platforms charge per message, per action or per task. Estimate monthly volume early; a cheap pilot can become an expensive rollout.

When signals pile up, move only the hard part into code behind an API, and keep the platform as the front door. That keeps the benefits (sign-in, channels, governance) while the logic gets tests and version control.

Edge case: dropping to code creates something the customer's makers cannot maintain. Agree who owns the API, where it is hosted and how it is monitored before you write it.
subtopics.example: The code scores three builds against signals. The policy Q&A agent stays low-code. The eligibility rules score 8, so the FDE moves them into a small tested API called through a custom connector, and the agent in Teams looks the same to users.
subtopics.code:
# Score a low-code build against signals that it should move (partly) to code
SIGNALS = {
    "needs unit tests for business rules": 3,
    "processes large files or many rows": 3,
    "hits run, timeout or payload limits": 3,
    "logic spread over more than 30 flow steps": 2,
    "needs sub-second response": 2,
    "cost per message growing faster than use": 2,
    "only one person can read the flow": 1,
}

def review(name, present):
    score = sum(SIGNALS[s] for s in present)
    verdict = ("move the hard part to an API" if score >= 6
               else "watch it" if score >= 3 else "keep it low-code")
    print(f"{name:18} score {score:2}  {verdict}")

review("Policy Q&A agent", [])
review("Leave balance", ["only one person can read the flow", "needs sub-second response"])
review("Eligibility rules", ["needs unit tests for business rules",
                              "logic spread over more than 30 flow steps",
                              "hits run, timeout or payload limits"])
# Output:
# Policy Q&A agent   score  0  keep it low-code
# Leave balance      score  3  watch it
# Eligibility rules  score  8  move the hard part to an API

subtopics.title: Handing a low-code build to citizen developers
subtopics.body:
Success on a low-code project means the customer's own people can run and change it after you leave. These people are often citizen developers: analysts or operations staff who build on the platform but are not professional engineers.

Decide the split early. Citizen developers usually own: knowledge sources, wording of instructions and answers, simple topics and flows, and adding new questions to the test set. Engineers own: custom connectors and APIs, authentication, anything touching payments or personal data, and moving changes to production.

Build for them from the start: clear names for every topic, flow and variable; short descriptions on each step; no clever tricks; one solution or package with everything in it; and environment variables instead of hard-coded URLs.

The handover pack: an overview diagram, a list of components with owners, the test set and how to run it, known limits, the runbook for common problems (see the runbook template in Docs), and who to call for the API.

Train with real changes: pair with a maker while they add a topic and publish it through test to production. Then let them do the next one while you watch. The Enablement topic covers champions and office hours in more depth.

Edge case: when the maker who built a flow leaves the company, flows tied to their personal account can stop. Use service accounts or shared ownership for production connections.
subtopics.example: At handover, an HR operations analyst adds a new topic about parental leave, tests it against 15 saved questions in the test environment, and publishes it through the pipeline. The FDE only reviews. The leave-balance API stays with the customer's integration team, who got its runbook.
checklist: Every topic, flow and variable has a clear name and description
All parts are in one solution or package, moved by a pipeline
Production connections use a service account, not a person
A saved test set of real questions runs before each publish
Owners are named for the agent, each connector and the API
Runbook and known limits are shared and walked through
A maker has published one real change end to end with you watching

glossary: Low-code platform
Software for building apps, workflows or agents mostly with visual designers and short formulas.
Citizen developer
A business user who builds on a low-code platform without being a professional developer. Also called a maker.
Connector
A prebuilt link that lets a platform read from or act on another system.
Custom connector
A connector you define yourself, usually from an OpenAPI file, to call your own API.
OpenAPI
A standard YAML or JSON format that describes an API's paths, inputs, outputs and authentication.
Topic
In agent builders, one job the agent handles, with its trigger and instructions.
Flow
An automated sequence of steps, such as a Power Automate flow or a Salesforce Flow.
Environment
A separate space on the platform, such as dev, test or production, with its own data and settings.
DLP policy
Data loss prevention rules that decide which connectors can be used together, or at all.
Solution
In Power Platform, a package holding all parts of a build so it can move between environments.
Service account
A non-person account used for production connections, so builds do not depend on one employee.
On-premises data gateway
Software that lets a cloud platform reach systems inside the customer's own network.
